content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by abnormal irreversible dilation and destruction of the bronchial tubes (airways) in the lungs. This structural damage impairs mucus clearance, leading to repeated lung infections and inflammation that perpetuate airway injury. Common synonyms include "chronic bronchial dilatation" and "non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis," which distinguish it from cystic fibrosis-related bronchiectasis. Bronchiectasis has diverse causes, including prior severe infections, immune deficiencies, genetic disorders (excluding cystic fibrosis), and airway obstructions. The impaired mucociliary clearance mechanism and distorted airway anatomy promote bacterial colonization and recurrent respiratory infections, worsening lung damage over time. Symptoms often include chronic productive cough, sputum production, breathlessness, recurrent chest infections, and fatigue. Diagnostic evaluation typically involves clinical history, sputum analysis, pulmonary function tests, and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scans of the chest, which visualize airway abnormalities. Management focuses on controlling infections, optimizing airway clearance through chest physiotherapy, inhaled and systemic medications, and treating underlying causes where possible. While a definitive cure is generally not possible, appropriate interventions can reduce symptoms, prevent exacerbations, and slow progression. Patient safety considerations include prompt treatment of infections and awareness of potential medication side effects. Bronchiectasis is a complex condition requiring multidisciplinary care tailored to the individual. Limitations in existing research include variability in disease presentation and response to therapies. Emerging evidence is clarifying phenotypes and novel therapies such as macrolide antibiotics for their anti-inflammatory effects. Overall, understanding bronchiectasis supports better symptom management and improves quality of life for affected individuals.

content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disorder characterized by permanent dilation and structural damage of the bronchi, the large passages that transport air into the lungs. The disease results from a cycle of airway inflammation, infection, and impaired mucus clearance. It differs from other lung diseases like asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in its structural and pathological features. Bronchiectasis may affect one or multiple lung lobes and varies considerably in severity and progression. Common synonyms include "chronic bronchial dilatation" and "non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis," the latter term distinguishing it from bronchiectasis arising from cystic fibrosis (CF).

content: Bronchiectasis arises due to a variety of causes that damage the airways or impair mucus clearance. Common causes include prior infections such as tuberculosis, pneumonia, or whooping cough that cause airway injury. Other causes encompass congenital disorders like primary ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiencies that reduce infection-fighting capacity, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), and airway obstruction from foreign bodies or tumors. In many cases, no specific cause is identified, termed idiopathic bronchiectasis. Understanding the underlying cause is critical for targeted management.

content: Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing bronchiectasis. These include a history of severe childhood respiratory infections, recurrent pneumonia or lung infections, immune system deficiencies, smoking, pollution exposure, and certain genetic disorders apart from cystic fibrosis. Patients with chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis may also be at increased risk. Early identification of risk factors can enable preventive measures and monitoring.

content: The main symptoms of bronchiectasis include a chronic productive cough with large amounts of sputum, shortness of breath, wheezing, chest pain, and frequent respiratory infections. Patients may report fatigue, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), and recurrent episodes of pneumonia. Symptoms often worsen during exacerbations triggered by infections. The clinical presentation can be variable in severity and progression between individuals.

content: Diagnosis of bronchiectasis begins with a detailed medical history and physical examination. Imaging is crucial; high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest is the gold standard and reveals characteristic airway dilation, wall thickening, and other structural changes. Pulmonary function tests assess airflow obstruction and lung capacity. Sputum cultures identify bacterial colonizers or infections. Additional tests may include blood work, immune function assessments, and tests for underlying causes such as cystic fibrosis or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

content: The pathophysiology of bronchiectasis involves a vicious cycle of impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic infection, and inflammation. Normally, cilia in airway cells transport mucus laden with debris and microbes out of the lungs. In bronchiectasis, damaged airways and ciliary dysfunction impair this clearance, allowing bacteria to thrive. Repeated infections induce inflammation, further degrading airway walls and perpetuating dilation and dysfunction. These mechanisms explain the typical persistent cough and infection susceptibility in patients.

content: Management of bronchiectasis aims to reduce symptoms, control infections, and prevent progression. Airway clearance techniques such as chest physiotherapy and mucus clearance devices are foundational. Antibiotics target acute infections and may be used prophylactically in some cases. Bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids can relieve symptoms, although evidence varies. Treatment of underlying conditions, immunizations, and smoking cessation are important. In severe or localized cases, surgical resection may be considered. Multidisciplinary care improves outcomes.

content: Patients with bronchiectasis benefit from lifestyle adaptations to maintain lung health. These include regular airway clearance exercises, avoiding respiratory irritants like smoke and pollution, maintaining adequate hydration, and engaging in physical activity within tolerance. Nutritional support and vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus reduce infection risks. Stress management and adherence to prescribed treatments are also vital for maintaining quality of life and preventing exacerbations.

content: Complications of bronchiectasis can include frequent lung infections, respiratory failure, hemoptysis, and development of other lung diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Some patients experience progressive lung damage leading to reduced lung function and disability. Early diagnosis and effective management improve prognosis, but the course can be variable. Monitoring and regular medical follow-up are essential to identify changes and complications promptly.

content: There are several misconceptions around bronchiectasis. One is that it is always caused by cystic fibrosis; in reality, many cases are non-CF related. Another is that bronchiectasis is contagious; it is not contagious but can increase susceptibility to infections which might be transmissible. Some believe bronchiectasis is curable; however, it is usually a chronic condition managed rather than cured. Educating patients and caregivers helps align expectations and promote proper care.
